g1-36.definition: A fresh-context agent, usually Opus at high effort, whose job is to disprove a claim, fix or design. It treats the claim as wrong until code, tests or sources show otherwise.

g2-163.definition: A machine-wide permit to run the clinic’s full check, so heavy checks wait their turn instead of colliding on this PC. The clinic set up two [S] slots but opened the second only when 8 GiB [S] of memory was free, which never happened, so in practice it had one, with waits up to 2,030 s [M]. FixFlow’s equivalent is a slot of ff-slot.sh (see ff-gates.sh / ff-slot.sh / slot).

g3-232.definition: Running a model many times with each unknown drawn from its range, to see the spread of outcomes and which unknowns matter most, instead of one answer.
g3-232.origin: General statistics; I proposed it for the library pathway map.

g1-99.definition: A second author, separate from Dex Horthy, who added skills to the HumanLayer repositories and gave a talk on loop engineering; 97 [M] of the 1,906 [M] sweep cards come from Kyle Mistele’s material.

add-18.definition: The six labels we give every idea. Idea: written down, not yet designed. Designed: a written design exists. Built: the mechanism exists but has not been measured. Tested: measured or tried at least once. In use: part of how we work now. Parked: set aside for now, ruled out or replaced, and kept with the reason. A label is the furthest stage any source reports, which stops a design being described as a result.
add-18.origin: This compile’s own honesty rule: a label never claims more than its sources report.

g1-93.definition: The eleven [M] artefacts the fitting ideas reduce to: 1 sealed replay, 2 verdict script, 3 transcript audit, 4 one finding table, 5 dry run with stand-in agents, 6 merge queue, 7 one fact, one command (facts backed by a command), 8 resume check, 9 fix-round clauses, 10 I read marked lines on high-risk merges, 11 a short tool list per agent.

add-6.definition: The low-cost tier (Sonnet, or Haiku for lookups) used for routine reading and checking, against the high-cost tiers (Opus and Fable) kept for judgement. The escalation ladder moves work up, from the cheap model to Opus to Fable, only when needed.

g1-20.definition: Claude Code’s multi-agent working mode: with it on, a session runs workflows of many agents by default, so token cost multiplies and the model and effort chosen for each agent matter.

g1-27.definition: A per-run log of finished agent results that lets a stopped workflow resume from its run id; knownDead lists ids that returned null last time. Not the same as the knowledge store’s journal of event files.

g2-171.definition: The list of files a slice declares it will write. The plan check uses it to avoid collisions between lanes. Not the same as a knowledge-store entry’s footprint.

g1-40.definition: A review result in a fixed machine-readable form that names the head commit the reviewer read. See also Output shapes and Verdicts.

g2-166.definition: The lane or worker count where the lowest limit is reached. Beyond it, more lanes or workers add queues and tokens but no speed. In the testbed the check’s knee was between 6 and 12 workers [M], and about three lanes [M] were worth running.

g3-241.definition: Planned retrieval thresholds: lead at 0.5 [S], candidate at 0.3 [S], margin 0.2 [S]. They decide lead, candidate or miss and are to be frozen at KS-4.

g2-141.definition: The planned adherence experiment: 10 [T] direct probes, which ask about a CLAUDE.md rule outright, plus oblique probes, all scored with a frozen rubric to see whether agents obey CLAUDE.md under different layouts or models. Planned, not yet run.

g1-95.definition: Our map of the 21 [M] clinic bottlenecks B01 to B21, each with a class, a first step and a proof, and of how the outside ideas fit them, in docs/program/HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11.md. Not to be confused with this compile (this document), which joins everything.

rd-1.definition: A way of modelling a system as stocks (things that pile up, such as waiting work), flows (rates in and out) and feedback loops, then running the model over time to see where queues form and what a change would do. We use it for the harness and the library, with loops R1 to R4 and B1 to B5.
rd-1.origin: A modelling method begun by Jay Forrester at MIT in the 1950s. Harness v2 and the library pathway map use it, because I asked to see the system as stocks, flows and loops with a runnable model.

addTerms.definition: Response-time percentiles. p50 is the median: half of the requests are faster. p95 is the time that 95 % of requests beat, so it shows the slow tail.

addTerms.definition: Repeating a held-out test at several split dates: each time, tune on the commits before the date and score on the commits after it, to see whether a result holds over time rather than for one split.

addTerms.definition: A location boundary around the shop. When a technician’s phone crosses it, the FixFlow app prompts an arrival or exit punch for attendance, even in the background.

addTerms.definition: Railway’s automatic build detector: it inspects a folder and decides how to build it. Run from the repository root it finds the web app, which is why the backend is deployed from backend/.

addTerms.definition: Supabase’s connection proxy. FixFlow’s backend reaches its Postgres database through it over IPv4.

addTerms.definition: Expo terms. A managed app lets Expo generate the native Android project at build time; a bare app keeps its own native folder, and Expo then skips its config plugins, the build-time add-ons that set permissions and native settings.

addTerms.definition: Windows can give a packaged app, such as the Claude desktop app, and the processes it starts their own private view of some AppData folders. Files written there can then differ from what my own shell sees at the same path, so a shared store must live elsewhere.
addTerms.origin: Windows MSIX app packaging; found as KS-F1 in the knowledge-store design.

addTerms.definition: Linux’s built-in hardware virtualisation. /dev/kvm is the device a Linux system needs to run a fast virtual machine such as the Android emulator; the svm flag shows an AMD processor supports it. Docker’s Linux VM on this PC does not expose it, so the emulator runs on Windows.
addTerms.origin: Linux kernel feature; found in the device-lab work (ship plan §7.5).

addTerms.definition: A fast Python package and environment manager. A throwaway uv environment is made for one job and deleted afterwards, so nothing is installed on the system.
addTerms.origin: Outside open-source tool (Astral).

addTerms.definition: The query language of graph databases such as Neo4j and LadybugDB: a query describes a pattern of nodes and links to find.
addTerms.origin: Created for Neo4j; now the openCypher standard.

addTerms.definition: Two more graph databases we could run through Docker: FalkorDB is a graph database server, and Apache AGE adds graph queries to Postgres.
addTerms.origin: Outside open-source projects.

addTerms.definition: A database index that holds every column a query needs, so the query is answered from the index without reading the table.
addTerms.origin: Standard database practice.

addTerms.definition: A terminal tool that runs several shell sessions in one window. One program can read or type into another’s session, which is how one Claude session can watch another.
addTerms.origin: Outside open-source tool.

addTerms.definition: In the library pathway model, how far the library route’s cost and wrong rate fall, on average, when every library unknown moves from its middle value to its good end: 30.6 % [G]. Step and limitation weights are shares of it.
addTerms.origin: Coined by us in model-brief.md (library pathway map), 2026-11.

addTerms.definition: The nine checkpoints, G0 to G8, of the clinic testbed’s planned measurement system (see M00-M06). They are not the G1 and G2 gates of the orchestration design.
addTerms.origin: Clinic testbed measurement design (A7-09 to A7-12).

addTerms.definition: The ten numbered findings of the clinic testbed’s effectiveness review. They proposed four separate measures (quality, context, productivity, cost), a context freshness test, a frozen baseline and a throwaway deployment with backup and restore.
addTerms.origin: Clinic testbed effectiveness review.

addTerms.definition: The running record of decisions, evidence and session ids that a phase keeps in its draft pull request’s description, so a later session can resume from it.
addTerms.origin: Our ship-plan practice; the harness review calls it the PR-body journal.

addTerms.definition: Expo’s over-the-air update feature, which can push new JavaScript to installed apps without a new build. FixFlow’s device rulings say not to use it.
addTerms.origin: Expo (outside open-source tool); FixFlow ship-plan rulings.

addTerms.definition: A crash-reporting service. The FixFlow mobile app sends crash reports to it only when a DSN, the project’s address, is set.
addTerms.origin: Outside vendor; CLAUDE.md (Mobile).

addTerms.definition: An open-source coding agent that runs in the terminal. Its repo map, a ranked outline of a codebase’s files and symbols sent to the model, is one source of our code-map ideas.
addTerms.origin: Outside open-source project.

addTerms.definition: A TypeScript educator, known for Total TypeScript. A Matt Pocock livestream is one of the Dex Horthy sweep’s sources.
addTerms.origin: Outside person; HARNESS-IDEAS-HORTHY-2026-11.md.

addTerms.definition: Free hosted notebook services with GPU time limits. Long training runs there can be cut off, much as a session limit stops an agent.
addTerms.origin: Google (Colab) and Kaggle, outside services.

addTerms.definition: A browser automation tool that can drive a web app and take screenshots.
addTerms.origin: Outside open-source project (Microsoft).

addTerms.definition: Two graph measures. Connected components are groups of nodes linked to one another; the k-core is the part of a graph where every node has at least k links, its densely connected centre.
addTerms.origin: Standard graph algorithms.

addTerms.definition: What a check does when it breaks. Fail open lets the action through; fail closed refuses it. Our edit hook fails open so a broken hook never blocks work; the privacy scrubber fails closed so nothing unscrubbed is written.
addTerms.origin: Standard reliability and security terms.

addTerms.definition: One of the nine groups the register sorts its bottlenecks into, such as Machine, Check, Review or Memory. Part 2 lists them, and the heat map in Part 3 counts the ideas aimed at each.
addTerms.origin: Coined by us in this compile.

addTerms.definition: A built-in Postgres view that lists the open sessions and what each one is waiting on.
addTerms.origin: PostgreSQL.

addTerms.definition: The one list of every bottleneck our sessions found, 128 [M] in all, joined and de-duplicated in Part 2; each row has a family, a state and the work package that answers it. Not the findings register of FixFlow’s reviews.
addTerms.origin: This compile, 13 November 2026. It joins the bottleneck compile’s B01 to B21, the harness v2 loops, the Dex Horthy sweep’s weaknesses and levers, and the ids added here.

addTerms.definition: A study that goes through one outside body of work idea by idea (each idea a card), scores every idea against our own weaknesses, sends the scores to refuters and sorts the survivors into adopt, trial and drop lists. We ran two: BAML (PR #184) and Dex Horthy (PR #186).
addTerms.origin: Our own term, from the sweeps of 4 and 9 November 2026.

addTerms.definition: Our 11 November design for the whole harness: eight parts (planner, scheduler, governor, lanes, gate, merge queue, library and machine), the feedback loops between them, five phases, eleven mechanisms and decisions D01 to D23. Part 1 sets it out.
addTerms.origin: docs/program/HARNESS-V2-DESIGN-2026-11.md, 11 November 2026.

addTerms.definition: Our held-out test of whether a typed code store (see that entry) finds what a change will touch better than search and simpler baselines, on commits the test had never seen. The typed store gained +0.076 [M] recall overall, with the gain in the mobile app.
addTerms.origin: docs/program/GRAPH-TEST-RESULT-2026-11.md, 12 to 13 November 2026.

addTerms.definition: Recording where a program spends its time, step by step, so the slow part can be found and cut. Tracing the clinic’s test start-up showed what to cut and made start-up 3.7× faster [M].
addTerms.origin: General software practice, also called profiling; used in the clinic testbed’s faster-check work.

addTerms.definition: A test sealed before any map or store is built: 5 [S] cases, 3 arms (a map, routed reading and Graphify), 2 [S] runs each and blind scoring; an arm counts as better only with a gap of 0.10 [S] in 4 of 5 cases. It keeps a pilot from being judged by rules chosen after the results.
addTerms.origin: Our library and graph-test work (idea MSR-18), kept by WP8.

addTerms.definition: A time when no FixFlow phase is running or waiting on its reviewer and no heavy check holds a slot on this PC, so a harness check or agent run cannot slow the ship lanes.
addTerms.origin: Our own term in this compile, from the harness v2 rule that the ship plan comes first.

addTerms.definition: The first-come order of FixFlow’s slot lock (ff-slot.sh): each waiting job drops a ticket and is served in arrival order. A light job may pass a heavier one only until the heavier one has waited 900 s [S], so neither kind can starve.
addTerms.origin: docs/program/lab/ff-slot.sh, added on 13 November 2026 after one lane waited 20 minutes [M] while later arrivals were served.

addTerms.definition: A Git Bash setting that stops it rewriting arguments that look like Unix paths into Windows paths. With it set, paths are written as C:/… .
addTerms.origin: MSYS2, the Unix layer under Git for Windows.

addTerms.definition: A git setting that lets Git for Windows create files whose full path is longer than Windows’ old limit of 260 characters. We pass it per command (git -c core.longpaths=true) when cloning into scratch folders.
addTerms.origin: Git for Windows.

addTerms.definition: One time the five-hour usage limit stopped agent work. October had 14 [M].
addTerms.origin: Our harness review and token measurement.

addTerms.definition: Replacing a file by writing the new version beside it and renaming it over the old one in a single step, so anything reading the file sees either the whole old version or the whole new one, never half of each.
addTerms.origin: Standard file-system practice; FixFlow’s gate scripts land changes this way so a running lane never reads a half-written script.

addTerms.definition: Every workflow is saved as a script before it runs, so it can be re-run and its result checked against the saved version.
addTerms.origin: Our orchestration design; adopted through WP10a.
